items.title: Two or more defaults
items.prose: A lender holds 50 loans. Each defaults this year with chance 0.02, independently.
items.question: What is the chance of at least 2 defaults? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take 1 minus the chances of 0 and of 1 default.

byKey.at-least-one: 0.6358 is the chance of at least one default. Also remove the chance of exactly one.
byKey.one-minus-one: You took $1 - P(X = 1)$. Remove $P(X = 0)$ as well.

explain.text: $P(X = 0) = 0.98^{50} \approx 0.3642$ and $P(X = 1) = 50 \times 0.02 \times 0.98^{49} \approx 0.3716$. So $P(X \ge 2) \approx 1 - 0.7358 = 0.2642$. That relies on independence, which a recession would break.

items.title: The mean of a Poisson
items.prose: Prove that $X \sim \text{Pois}(\lambda)$ has $E[X] = \lambda$, straight from the pmf.
items.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

feedback.correct: Cancel the $k$, pull out a $\lambda$, and the rest is a whole pmf.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the definition and aim to make the sum a full Poisson pmf.

byKey.end: Summing to 1 needs the sum written as a full pmf first, so it comes last.

explain.text: Cancelling $k$ against $k!$ and pulling out one $\lambda$ leaves the Poisson pmf summed over all $j$. That sum is 1, so $E[X] = \lambda$. The same trick on $E[X(X - 1)]$ gives $\lambda^2$, hence $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \lambda$.

items.title: Memory and the mean
items.prose: A limit order fills in each minute with chance 0.2, independently. It has already waited 3 minutes without a fill.
items.question: What is the expected minute of the fill, counted from when the order was placed?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use memorylessness: from minute 3 the wait starts afresh.

byKey.remaining: 5 is the mean of the remaining wait. Add the 3 minutes already gone.
byKey.failures: You added the mean number of failures, 4. The remaining wait includes the fill: 5 minutes.
byKey.waited: 3 is the time already spent. The fill is still to come.

explain.text: Given $X > 3$, the remaining wait $X - 3$ is again $\text{Geo}(0.2)$, with mean 5. So $E[X \mid X > 3] = 3 + 5 = 8$. The 3 minutes already spent are sunk; they do not shorten the rest.

items.title: A shorter window
items.prose: Large orders arrive at 3 an hour on average, independently.
items.question: What is the chance of no large order in a 10-minute window?

widget.label: Chance of no order in 10 minutes

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Scale the rate to the window, then use $e^{-\lambda}$.

byKey.linear: You took $1 - 0.5$. The chance of none is $e^{-0.5}$, not $1 - \lambda$.
byKey.sixth: You divided the hourly answer by 6. Scale $\lambda$ instead.

explain.text: Ten minutes is a sixth of an hour, so $\lambda = 0.5$. Then $P(X = 0) = e^{-0.5} \approx 0.6065$. Scale the rate, never the probability.

items.title: Checking a batch of trades
items.prose: A batch of 50 trades contains 5 booked wrongly. A controller checks 10, chosen at random, all different.
items.question: What is the chance she finds at least one bad trade? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of finding a bad trade

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance all 10 checks are clean, then take the complement.

byKey.binomial: $1 - 0.9^{10}$ treats the checks as independent. Without replacement each clean check raises the next one's chance of a bad trade.
byKey.none: 0.3106 is the chance she finds none.
byKey.added: You added ten chances of 0.1. The events overlap, so use the complement.

explain.text: All clean has chance $\binom{45}{10} / \binom{50}{10} \approx 0.3106$, so at least one bad trade is found with chance 0.6894. The binomial $1 - 0.9^{10} = 0.6513$ understates it. Each clean check leaves the bad trades a larger share of what is left.

items.title: Waiting for two lucky passes
items.prose: A researcher backtests no-edge variants, each passing by luck with chance $p$, independently. She stops at the second pass. Let $T$ be the total number of backtests.
items.question: Write $E[T]$ in terms of $p$.

feedback.correct: $E[T] = 2/p$: two geometric waits back to back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Split $T$ into the wait for the first pass and the wait after it.

byKey.square: $1/p^2$ multiplies the two waits. Waits back to back add.
byKey.half: You halved the mean. A second pass needs more backtests, not fewer.
byKey.one: $1/p$ is the wait for one pass. She waits for two.

explain.text: Write $T = W_1 + W_2$: the wait for the first pass, then the wait from there to the second. By memorylessness $W_2$ is a fresh $\text{Geo}(p)$. Linearity gives $E[T] = 1/p + 1/p = 2/p$, so 40 backtests at $p = 0.05$.

items.title: Defaults that move together
items.prose: A credit model treats defaults among 200 loans as $\text{Bin}(200, 0.02)$, with mean 4 and variance 3.92. Over 20 years, the yearly default counts had mean 4 but variance 15.
items.question: What is the best reading of this?

options.text: Defaults are not independent: they cluster in bad years, so the model understates bad years
The model is fine, because the mean matches
options.why: You checked only the mean. The variance is nearly four times what the binomial allows.

options.text: The default chance $p$ is wrong; raise it to fix the variance
options.why: Raising $p$ raises the mean too, which already matches. The extra spread comes from dependence.
A Poisson has variance 4, no closer to 15. It assumes independence too.

feedback.correct: Variance far above $np(1 - p)$ means the trials move together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the observed variance with $np(1 - p)$.

explain.text: Independent trials would give variance near $200 \times 0.02 \times 0.98 = 3.92$. A variance of 15 means defaults arrive together, as in a recession. Covariances between loans are positive, and the binomial sets them to zero.

items.title: At most one loss
items.prose: A strategy has 10 independent trades a day, each losing with chance 0.1.
items.question: What is the chance of at most one losing trade in a day? Give 4 decimal places.

widget.label: Chance of at most one loss

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $P(X = 0)$ and $P(X = 1)$ for $\text{Bin}(10, 0.1)$.

byKey.none: That is $P(X = 0)$ alone. At most one includes exactly one.
byKey.one: 0.3874 is $P(X = 1)$ alone, and also what you get if you drop the factor $\binom{10}{1} = 10$. Add the chance of no loss, with the factor kept.

explain.text: $P(X = 0) = 0.9^{10} \approx 0.3487$ and $P(X = 1) = \binom{10}{1} 0.1 \times 0.9^9 \approx 0.3874$. The sum is about 0.7361. Dropping the factor 10 from the second term would give only 0.3874.

items.title: The variance without replacement
items.prompt:
A population of $N$ items holds $K$ marked ones. You draw $n$ without replacement and let $X$ be the number of marked items drawn. Write $p = K/N$.

1. Using indicators $I_1, \ldots, I_n$, show that $E[X] = np$.
2. Find $\operatorname{Cov}(I_i, I_j)$ for $i \ne j$.
3. Show that $\operatorname{Var}(X) = np(1 - p)\dfrac{N - n}{N - 1}$.
4. Check your formula on the audit: $N = 20$, $K = 4$, $n = 5$. Say in one sentence why the variance is below the binomial's.
items.model:
**1. Mean.** Let $I_i = 1$ if the $i$th item drawn is marked. By symmetry the $i$th draw is equally likely to be any of the $N$ items, so $P(I_i = 1) = K/N = p$. Then $X = I_1 + \cdots + I_n$ and linearity gives $E[X] = np$. Linearity needs no independence.

**2. Covariance.** For $i \ne j$, the pair of draws is equally likely to be any ordered pair of distinct items, so $$P(I_i = 1, I_j = 1) = \frac{K}{N} \cdot \frac{K - 1}{N - 1}.$$ Hence $$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(I_i, I_j) &= \frac{K(K - 1)}{N(N - 1)} - \frac{K^2}{N^2} \\ &= -\frac{K(N - K)}{N^2(N - 1)} \\ &= -\frac{p(1 - p)}{N - 1}. \end{aligned}$$

**3. Variance.** Each $\operatorname{Var}(I_i) = p(1 - p)$, since $I_i$ is Bernoulli. The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances plus every covariance, and there are $n(n - 1)$ ordered pairs: $$\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(X) &= np(1 - p) \\ &\quad - n(n - 1)\frac{p(1 - p)}{N - 1} \\ &= np(1 - p)\left(1 - \frac{n - 1}{N - 1}\right) \\ &= np(1 - p)\frac{N - n}{N - 1}. \end{aligned}$$

**4. Check.** With $p = 0.2$: $5 \times 0.2 \times 0.8 \times \tfrac{15}{19} = 0.8 \times \tfrac{15}{19} \approx 0.6316$. Summing $(k - 1)^2 P(X = k)$ over the pmf $0.2817, 0.4696, 0.2167, 0.0310, 0.0010$ gives the same 0.6316. The variance is below the binomial's 0.8 because the indicators are negatively correlated: each marked item drawn leaves fewer to draw.

rubric.text: Defines the indicators and writes $X$ as their sum.
Argues $P(I_i = 1) = K/N$ by symmetry and gets $E[X] = np$ by linearity.
Simplifies the covariance to $-\tfrac{p(1 - p)}{N - 1}$ (or an equal form).
Adds variances and the $n(n - 1)$ covariances, and simplifies to the stated formula.
Explains the smaller variance by negative correlation between draws.

items.title: A capped wait, two ways
items.prompt:
A trader rests a limit order. In each minute it fills with chance $p$, where $0 < p < 1$. The chance is the same every minute, and the minutes are independent. If the order has not filled by the end of minute $m$, a whole number $m \ge 1$, she cancels it. Let $T$ be the number of minutes the order rests: the minute it fills, or $m$ if it is cancelled. Write $q = 1 - p$.

(a) Find the distribution of $T$, and check that its chances add to 1.

(b) Derive $E[T]$ by conditioning on the first minute.

(c) Derive $E[T]$ again, this time by summing the series from (a). Show that the two answers agree.

(d) Take $p = 0.15$ and $m = 10$. Find the chance that the order is cancelled, and find $E[T]$. Optional, one more point: say what $E[T]$ tends to as $m \to \infty$, and why.

Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**Setting.** Each minute is a trial that fills with chance $p$, independently of the others. Let $X$ be the minute of the first fill, so $X \sim \text{Geo}(p)$ and $T = \min(X, m)$.

**(a)** Take $k$ with $1 \le k \le m - 1$. Then $T = k$ exactly when minutes 1 to $k - 1$ do not fill and minute $k$ fills. Independent chances multiply, so $P(T = k) = q^{k-1}p$.

$T = m$ exactly when minutes 1 to $m - 1$ do not fill. Minute $m$ may then fill or not: either way the order rests $m$ minutes. So $P(T = m) = q^{m-1}$, and no other value is possible.

The chances add to 1. Let $G = 1 + q + \cdots + q^{m-2}$, an empty sum (0) when $m = 1$. Then $G - qG = 1 - q^{m-1}$, since every middle power appears once in each and cancels. As $1 - q = p$, $G = \tfrac{1 - q^{m-1}}{p}$. So
$$\sum_{k=1}^{m-1} q^{k-1}p + q^{m-1} = pG + q^{m-1} = 1.$$

**(b)** Write $e_m$ for $E[T]$ when the cap is $m$. With a cap of 1 the order always rests 1 minute, so $e_1 = 1$. Now let $m \ge 2$ and condition on minute 1.

- It fills, with chance $p$. Then $T = 1$.
- It does not, with chance $q$. One minute is used. Minutes 2, 3, ... are independent of minute 1, and each fills with chance $p$. So from minute 2 on, the order is a fresh order with $m - 1$ minutes left, and $E[T \mid \text{no fill in minute 1}] = 1 + e_{m-1}$.

Averaging the two conditional means with their chances,
$$e_m = p \cdot 1 + q\,(1 + e_{m-1}) = 1 + q\,e_{m-1}.$$
Setting $e_0 = 0$ makes this hold at $m = 1$ as well. Applying it again and again,
$$\begin{aligned} e_m &= 1 + q\,(1 + q\,e_{m-2}) = \cdots \\ &= 1 + q + \cdots + q^{m-1} + q^m e_0. \end{aligned}$$
The last term is 0. The same subtraction as in (a) gives $1 + q + \cdots + q^{m-1} = \tfrac{1 - q^m}{1 - q}$. So
$$E[T] = \frac{1 - q^m}{p}.$$

**(c)** From (a), $E[T]$ is each value times its chance:
$$E[T] = \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} k\,q^{k-1}p + m\,q^{m-1}.$$
Let $S = \sum_{k=1}^{m-1} k\,q^{k-1}$. Multiplying by $q$ and shifting the index, $qS = \sum_{k=2}^{m} (k - 1)\,q^{k-1}$. Now subtract term by term. The $k = 1$ term of $S$ leaves 1. Each $k$ from 2 to $m - 1$ leaves $k\,q^{k-1} - (k - 1)\,q^{k-1} = q^{k-1}$. The last term of $qS$, $(m - 1)\,q^{m-1}$, is taken away. So
$$(1 - q)\,S = G - (m - 1)\,q^{m-1},$$
with $G = \tfrac{1 - q^{m-1}}{p}$ from (a). As $1 - q = p$, $pS = \tfrac{1 - q^{m-1}}{p} - (m - 1)\,q^{m-1}$. Adding the cap term $m\,q^{m-1}$,
$$\begin{aligned} E[T] &= \frac{1 - q^{m-1}}{p} + q^{m-1} \\ &= \frac{1 - q^{m-1} + p\,q^{m-1}}{p} \\ &= \frac{1 - q^{m-1}\,q}{p} = \frac{1 - q^m}{p}, \end{aligned}$$
using $1 - p = q$ in the last line. This is the answer from (b).

**(d)** The order is cancelled when none of the 10 minutes fills, with chance $q^{10} = 0.85^{10} \approx 0.1969$. This is not $P(T = 10) = 0.85^9 \approx 0.2316$, which also counts a fill in minute 10. And
$$\begin{aligned} E[T] &= \frac{1 - 0.85^{10}}{0.15} \approx \frac{0.8031}{0.15} \\ &\approx 5.354 \text{ minutes}. \end{aligned}$$
As $m \to \infty$, $q^m \to 0$ because $0 < q < 1$. So $E[T] \to \tfrac1p$, the mean of the uncapped geometric wait: $\tfrac{1}{0.15} \approx 6.667$ minutes here. The cap takes about 1.31 minutes off the mean wait, at the cost of a cancelled order about one time in five.

rubric.text: (a) Tick only if all are given: $P(T = k) = q^{k-1}p$ for $k < m$, from independent minutes; $P(T = m) = q^{m-1}$, which includes a fill in minute $m$; and the chances shown to add to 1.

(b) Conditions on minute 1 and says why the order is then a fresh one with $m - 1$ minutes left (independent minutes, the same chance). Gets $e_m = 1 + q\,e_{m-1}$ with a starting value, and solves it to $\tfrac{1 - q^m}{p}$ with the geometric sum justified.

(c) Writes $E[T]$ from the distribution, including the term $m\,q^{m-1}$. Sums the finite series with each step justified (shift and subtract, or another valid route) and reaches $\tfrac{1 - q^m}{p}$, the answer from (b).
(d) Gives the cancel chance $0.85^{10} \approx 0.1969$, not $0.85^9$, and $E[T] \approx 5.354$ minutes.
